item.title: The Invisible Prisoner: Why We Can See Trapped Water but Not Trapped Light
item.author: hari@dasarpai.com (Dr. Hari Thapliyaal)
item.description:
The Invisible Prisoner: Why We Can See Trapped Water but Not Trapped Light
#

Part 29 of the Learning Quantum Physics series.

A seed scatters lamp light and stays inside the crystal. A stored photon does not. You see it when it leaves, or from a second object that met the field.

Quantum Gates: Matrices, Mirrors, and Beam Splitters follows one photon through glass. Quantum Measurement, Randomness, and Everyday Technology says what a detector does when a photon arrives. This article asks whether light itself can sit in a cage, and whether you can see it while it is still inside.

item.title: Quantum Gates: Matrices, Mirrors, and Beam Splitters
item.author: hari@dasarpai.com (Dr. Hari Thapliyaal)
item.description:
Quantum Gates: Matrices, Mirrors, and Beam Splitters
#

Part 28 of the Learning Quantum Physics series.

A quantum gate is a matrix multiplied by the qubit column. On one photon that matrix is a mirror, a glass plate, a wave plate, or a beam splitter.

On one photon, the same rule is a piece of hardware. A mirror can swap two paths. A glass plate can change the phase of one path. A beam splitter can mix the two paths. A wave plate does the matching job when the qubit is the direction of the light wave.

This article gives each standard gate three things: the matrix, one use, and the piece of glass. Operators in Quantum Mechanics sorts a matrix into a gate, a measurement instruction, or a projector. Building a 20-Qubit Quantum System Using Photons builds a larger optical machine. Start here when the word gate is new.
